prime.problem: PagedAttention frees a request's KV the moment it finishes. But the next turn of the same chat, the next few-shot question or the next sample of the same question starts with the same tokens, and pays their prefill again: 32.5 ms and 262 MB for a 2,000-token system prompt on Llama-3.1-8B, every time.
prime.fits: First card on reusing KV across requests. It builds on paging (block size 1 here) and on paged II's copy-on-write sharing, and replaces "provider lists the shared prefixes" with a tree that finds them automatically.
expect: KV depends only on the prefix
radix tree: edges are runs of tokens
hit rate = cached prompt tokens ÷ prompt tokens
prime.goal: Replay a request trace on a radix tree by hand, compute its hit rate, and explain why leaf-first LRU keeps shared prefixes without pinning them.

attend: Why can a later request reuse an earlier one's KV bit for bit, and what breaks that if a single earlier token differs?
When a new chat shares only the system prompt with a cached one, what happens to the node that held both?
Why does evicting leaves first protect a shared system prompt without any special pinning?
What stops the cache from evicting KV that a running request is reading right now?
Why does a block-hash cache (vLLM style) miss some hits that a radix tree catches?

must: A token's K and V depend only on the tokens before it → requests sharing the first n tokens share that KV exactly → keep finished requests' KV keyed by their token sequence → a later match skips prefill for the matched part

Store sequences in a radix tree (edges = runs of tokens) → matching a new prompt is a walk from the root, splitting an edge where it diverges → any shared prefix is found automatically, at token granularity, at many levels (system prompt → examples → question → samples)

Cache and running batch share one pool → when short, evict least-recently-used leaves with reference count 0 → shared prefixes are ancestors, so they're evicted only after everything below them → system prompts survive; running requests are never touched
elevated: Block-hash caching only caches full blocks and matches block by block → hits end at the last full shared block → 57.4% vs the tree's 77.7% on the lab trace with 16-token blocks (the gap is small with long prompts)
reference: the exact node letters of Fig 3
the lab trace's token counts and 140-slot pool

compress.prompt: From memory, draw a radix tree for three requests: two chats sharing a system prompt and a few-shot query sharing nothing. Mark which node LRU evicts first and why the system prompt survives.
checklist: root → system prompt → one branch per chat's turns; a separate branch for the few-shot query
new requests walk the tree; divergence splits an edge
leaves with ref = 0 are evicted oldest first
an ancestor only becomes evictable once it is a leaf
hit rate counts prompt tokens only

retrieve.q: Explain why the KV of a shared prefix is reusable exactly, not approximately.
answer: each layer's K and V at position t depend only on tokens 0 … t
two requests with the same first n tokens compute identical values for those n positions
so the second can use the first's KV bit for bit

retrieve.q: Walk through step 4 of the trace: chat 2 arrives sharing only the system prompt with chat 1. What does the tree do, and what gets computed?
answer: the match walks the edge holding system prompt + chat 1's first turn and diverges after the system prompt
the edge is split into a system-prompt node with two children
20 of chat 2's 26 prompt tokens are cached; only its own turn is prefilled

retrieve.q: Compare an exact-match prompt cache, a block-hash prefix cache and a radix tree on chat traffic. Which misses what, and what does each cost?
answer: exact match only hits identical prompts, so a chat's next turn always misses (21.5% on the trace)
block hashing shares prefixes but only in full blocks (57.4%)
the radix tree matches to the exact token (77.7% unlimited, 64.6% in 140 slots) at the cost of a CPU tree walk (< 0.3% overhead in the paper)

compare.q: Paged II shares KV with reference counts and copy-on-write within a request or for provider-listed prefixes. What does RadixAttention add, and what does it borrow unchanged?
answer: borrows: paged KV (block size 1), reference counts, one shared pool
adds: keeping finished requests' KV, a tree index to find any shared prefix automatically, LRU eviction
so sharing happens across unrelated requests, not only inside one

compare.q: API providers sell "prompt caching" to clients. How does that relate to the radix tree here, and why does the client see it only if the prefix is identical and placed first?
answer: it is server-side prefix caching of the KV
KV depends on every earlier token, so only an identical leading prefix can match
reordering or editing anything early in the prompt invalidates everything after it

predict.q: The trace runs FCFS. Suppose 100 users each send one question after the same 1,500-token few-shot template, but their requests arrive interleaved with 100 users of 7 other templates, and the cache holds only 3 templates. Will LRU keep your template cached between its requests? Commit first.
predict.answer: Often not. With 8 templates cycling through a cache that holds 3, LRU evicts each template just before its next request arrives, and it is recomputed again and again: cache thrashing. The tree and LRU are fine; the order is the problem. That's the next card: sort waiting requests by longest cached prefix.

apply.task: Replay this trace by hand on an unlimited radix tree. Tokens: system prompt S = 100, questions Q1, Q2, Q3 = 20 each, every answer = 30. r1 = S + Q1. r2 = S + Q1 + A1 + Q2 (the chat's second turn). r3 = S + Q3. r4 = S + Q3 (a second sample of the same question). For each request write the matched (cached) prompt tokens, then the hit rate, and the same for an exact-match cache. Finally convert the saved tokens into a prefill-time floor with the course's 16.2 ms per 1,000 tokens.
apply.done: You have four matched counts, both hit rates and the time saved, and you can say which request only the radix tree catches.
apply.hint: Prompt tokens: 120 + 170 + 120 + 120 = 530. Radix: 0, 150 (S + Q1 + A1), 100 (S), 120 → 370 / 530 = 69.8%. Exact match: only r4 = 120 / 530 = 22.6%. 370 tokens × 16.2 ms / 1,000 ≈ 6.0 ms saved (our arithmetic). r2 and r3 are caught only by prefix matching.
